implementation_notes: Enumerator.produce(initial) { |state| next_state } is literally the unfold: it returns a lazy Enumerator whose block computes the next state, and stopping is expressed with a termination predicate in the pipeline (lazy.take_while) or a break in the producer. Chaining .lazy keeps the intermediate stages lazy - note that a bare Enumerator#take_while materializes an Array - and Enumerable#inject performs the fold in the same pass, so no Array is ever built. The enumerator can be re-run (each terminal method restarts the producer), which is convenient but re-executes the unfold; use Enumerator.new when a step must emit several values, and a plain loop for trivial arithmetic.
code_sketch:
def factorial(n)
  Enumerator.produce(n) { |s| s - 1 }        # unfold: n, n-1, ... (infinite)
            .lazy                            # keep the pipeline lazy
            .take_while { |s| s > 0 }        # termination predicate
            .inject(1) { |acc, s| acc * s }  # fold: fused, no Array built
end
pitfalls: Enumerator.produce is infinite by design, so every fold needs a take_while, a lazy-take or a break inside the producer - otherwise the process spins forever.
Enumerator#take_while returns an Array (materializing the whole prefix); only Enumerator::Lazy#take_while keeps the pipeline fused.
inject(:*) on an empty enumerator returns nil and with a single element returns that element unchanged; pass an explicit initial value so the terminal case has an identity.

variants.name: Explicit while loop with accumulator (pre-2.7 style)
variants.idiom_name: while loop stepping the seed and folding into the accumulator
variants.implementation_notes: Before Enumerator.produce - and whenever the generator is a trivial counter - the fused form is an explicit loop: recompute the next state and fold it into the accumulator in the same iteration, with the loop condition as the termination test. It allocates nothing, profiles trivially and stays the clearest form for arithmetic, whereas Enumerator.new { |y| loop { y << state } } is the middle ground: a hand-written lazy enumerator that composes with Enumerable methods but costs more code than the loop it replaces. Choose the enumerator form when the generated sequence is an API, the loop when it is an implementation detail.
variants.code_sketch:
def factorial(n)
  acc = 1
  while n > 0            # seed in n, accumulator in acc: one pass
    acc *= n             # fold now; no Array in between
    n -= 1               # next seed
  end
  acc
end
pitfalls: Mutating the seed in place is fine for numbers but destructive for objects: copy the seed first if the caller still needs it (a mutated Hash/Array is a shared-state bug).
Accumulator type is not enforced - a Float accumulator loses precision while Ruby promotes integers to Bignum silently.
A loop that also pushes intermediate values into an array 'for debugging' reintroduces the materialized structure the pattern exists to avoid.
